essentialQuestion.source: How can you check a photo, video or voice before you trust it?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you check a photo, video or audio before believing it?

learningGoal.source: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, tell labelled creative work from a fake, and check the source before you trust or share one.
learningGoal.back: Explain how AI makes realistic pictures, videos and audio, tell labelled creative work apart from fakes, and check the source before believing or sharing.

read.sections.0.heading.source: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI can make pictures, videos and audio

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add effects and teachers make lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. Labels can get lost, too. If someone shares the goat video without its label, as if it were real, it can mislead people.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI tools can make new pictures, videos and audio. These tools learned from huge numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively: artists make pictures, filmmakers add special effects and teachers make lessons, saying AI helped. In Greenhill the comedy club posted a talking-goat video with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so this video is not a trick. A fake is different, because it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often used to trick people for money or attention. Labels can disappear too: if someone shares the goat video without the label as if it were real, that video could mislead people.
read.sections.0.text.note: "label" on a post ("Made with AI") as ป้ายกำกับ, the KEY_TERMS word for a data label (DW03, DW05). A reviewer may prefer คำบอก or ข้อความกำกับ for a caption on social media.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Strange details are clues, not proof
read.sections.1.heading.back: Strange details are clues, not proof

read.sections.1.text.source: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
read.sections.1.text.back: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign, or a background that blends into a wall. In videos, mouths may not move in time with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake may look perfect. Real photos can look strange too, for example when blurred or taken in low light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They mistook about a quarter of real photos for AI pictures, and also missed about a quarter of AI pictures. The fruit seller picture has very smooth skin, but the photography club says who took it, and that it was taken with a phone.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, more than 50,000 people looked at pictures online. Some were real, and some were AI. People called about one in four real photos AI-made. They also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But the photo club says a phone took it.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, such as six fingers or messy letters. These are clues, but clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real pictures can look strange too, when they are dark or unclear. In a 2025 study more than 50,000 people looked at pictures online. Some were real pictures; AI made some. People thought about a quarter of the real pictures were made by AI. They also missed about a quarter of the AI pictures. The fruit seller has very smooth skin, but the photography club says it was taken with a phone.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: "one in four" written in words (หนึ่งในสี่) for reading aloud. The sentence about people misjudging pictures was split to stay short.

read.sections.2.text.source: So the most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does the maker say how it was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy one post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, and a page with no name posted the photo. So that photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.text.back: So the most useful way to check is to look at the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does the maker say how it was made? Do other trustworthy sources show the same thing? Make sure those sources did not all copy the same post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work with pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill the farm's own page says it did not grow giant pumpkins, and a page with no name posted the picture, so the picture is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still cannot tell, say plainly that you cannot tell yet, and do not share it yet.

watch.summary.source: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
watch.summary.back: This video is from a series made with a team of teen fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and audio, often for money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures may have strange hands, strange shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for blurry or flickering edges, check shadows, and see if lips move in time with the words. For AI audio, listen to the tone of voice and the background sounds. The video also shows tools that can help, such as a search that finds where else the same picture appears on the internet. But these tools are not always right; people still need to think and check before sharing.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Deepfakes are used to harm real people, such as fake pictures that humiliate people, fake videos of leaders and cloned voices used in scams (such as calls that sound like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). This lesson deliberately uses silly, light examples. Do not show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says someone made a fake of them or someone they know, do not discuss details in class; follow the partner organisation's own child-safeguarding procedures.

educatorNotes.0.source: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether the maker says how it was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and didn't all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. The study in section 2 is Kamali and others (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made and 149 real images; they called real photographs real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged each way. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source tells you; there is no sorting task.
educatorNotes.0.back: Teach checking first: who posted, when, where it first came from, whether the maker says how it was made, whether other trustworthy sources show the same thing (and did not all copy the same post), and for audio, contact the person another way. Visible flaws (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are a reason to check, not proof, because newer tools make fewer mistakes and real photos can have strange details. The study in part 2 is Kamali et al. (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made pictures and 149 real ones. They called real photos real in 74 percent of observations and AI pictures AI in 76 percent, so about a quarter were misjudged each way. This is one online study with the researchers' own picture set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a good answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source says. There is no sorting activity.

educatorNotes.1.source: Labelled AI work (art, film effects, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
educatorNotes.1.back: Labelled AI work (art, film special effects, lessons, or jokes clearly marked “made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels may disappear when someone reposts a picture (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can mislead when shared without the label. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check pictures and videos that spread widely, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). Teachers with internet might show one checked example; learners do not need to go online.
